newsitem.title: POLAND: Poles queue as mass privatisation scheme kicks in.
newsitem.headline: Poles queue as mass privatisation scheme kicks in.

text.p: Poland's mass privatisation programme reached a crucial phase on Friday as Poles queued in a last-minute rush to buy certificates in the programme's 15 National Investment Funds (NFI) as they gear up for bourse entry.

Friday saw the expiry of the one-year period during which 28 million eligible adult Poles could buy NFI units from the state. At a cost of 20 zlotys ($7.11), each NFI unit will later be exchangeable for one share in each of the 15 funds run by international management firms.

So far more than 24 million Poles have bought certificates and for the past two weeks people have been lining up outside branches of state-owned Bank PKO BP. More than 25 million people are estimated to have bought certificates.
NFI units closed on Thursday at 154 zlotys on the Warsaw bourse.
Analysts said the certificates could continue bringing profits once converted into listed fund shares, although it is too early to back this opinion with reliable information.
Malgorzata Dominiczak-Zielinska, an analyst at Pioneer Polski Dom Maklerski SA brokerage, said the units were worth 170 to 230 zlotys, representing a discount of 50 percent to currently listed firms.
Stephen Pettyfer, an analyst at Merrill Lynch in London, said it would be easier to appraise the funds once their issue prospectuses were published, and when 1997 data was available.

Deputy treasury minister Wieslaw Kaczmarek has said he hopep the ministry would submit issue a prospectus for each of the 15 NFIs to the Polish Securities Commission by mid-December and that the funds be would cleared for public trade by early March.
The listing of the funds is seen in the second quarter after which the funds, some of the 512 firms in the programme, and the units now traded would all be listed on the Warsaw bourse.
The treasury ministry has yet to announce the start of the one-year period over which the paper certificates would remain valid.
The ministry has estimated that more than 100 of the scheme's firms would be fit for either a bourse listing or trade on the nascent regulated over-the-counter market.
So far shares in construction materials maker Izolacja SA and wood firm Grajewo SA have been approved for public trade.
Analysts said it would take some time before the effects of the programme would filter down to individual companies, resulting in better management and higher competitiveness.
"In terms of the actual fund managers being able to roll up their sleeves and produce results -- I think it's a little early for that," said Pettyfer.

Kaczmarek, who as privatisation minister before a government reorganisation last month oversaw the launch of the scheme, said that even though the programme had yet to prove an economic success, it was already a political feat.

"The distribution phase obviously was a success -- whether it will be an economic success we will see in one and a half to two years...but now it is certainly a defeat to NFI opponents," he told journalists earlier this week.
Critics say the programme yields too much control over a large chunk of the economy to foreign fund managers. Firms' assets in the scheme were estimated to be worth over $3 billion.
The management firms are supervised by Polish-dominated supervisory boards but critics say their control is illusory.
Some sceptics say fund managers, eager to maximise market value of their assets as quickly as possible, might neglect the long-term task of turning around some of the weaker firms. ($1=2.8125 Zloty)
